A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VAP research work. The main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–G are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: V2 reports original simulation and real-world manipulation results in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5, together with appendix ablations and diagnostic analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds empirical evaluations of implicit instructions, visual prompting alternatives, occlusion, mask corruption, and dual-object commands.

M1.justification: The core detection, reference matching, SAM2 tracking, and frozen-VLA prompting procedure remains unchanged. V3 adds a tested GPT-4o-mini parser for implicit references (Appendix A.3) and parallel grounding with distinct tints for jointly referenced objects (Appendix F), extending v2's deterministic parsing and sequential single-mask execution.

E1.justification: The datasets, robots, and principal object categories are retained. Coverage expands within these settings to implicit referring expressions, controlled complete target occlusion, and five real-world commands jointly referencing two personal objects. V2 already evaluated sequential multi-user requests; simultaneous relational commands are the new requirement.

E2.justification: The visual-prompt comparison expands substantially from v2 Table 13 to v3 Table 17: new evaluated alternatives include opaque masks labelled RoboGround, points, circles, TraceVLA-style trajectory arrows, and PIVOT/MOKA-style numbered markers. These are prompting strategies evaluated within the shared frozen VLA, rather than demonstrated reproductions of the complete cited systems. The original generic, soft-prompt, and hard-prompt comparators remain.

E3.justification: V3 adds several evaluation designs: implicit-instruction parsing accuracy and task success, a 0–6-frame occlusion sweep with target-reassociation accuracy, mask erosion/dilation ratios from 0.25 to 2.0, and 100 dual-object trials across five instructions. These substantially extend the testing procedures. Tables 8–10 mainly document retained benchmark settings rather than establish changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: V2 already contains instruction-rewriting, reference-aggregation, reference-count, and prompt-design ablations, plus attention and error analyses. V3 expands prompt-design comparisons and adds parser-swappability verification, controlled tracking robustness under occlusion, and sensitivity to segmentation-mask corruption (Appendices A.3 and E.4–E.6), substantially broadening diagnostic evidence.

E5.justification: The ten-run reporting in Tables 3–4, across-task standard-deviation bars in Figure 5, and embedding-similarity uncertainty reporting are retained. V3 introduces no new seed disclosure, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation practice. Additional trial counts describe evaluation sample sizes.

E6.justification: Matched main benchmark scores in Tables 2–4 and Figure 5 remain unchanged. Substantial new results include 94.7–99.6% parsing accuracy in Table 7, additional prompt-comparator scores in Table 17, occlusion and mask-corruption results in Tables 18–19, and 60.0–75.0% success on dual-object commands in Table 21. These are additional findings under new conditions, not improvements to the retained benchmark scores.

T1.justification: The grounding/prompting formulation and reference-voting equation in Section 3 are retained, as are Appendix D.2's proposed cross-view association formulations. Expanded explanations introduce no substantive mathematical revision, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract, principal contribution bullets, and conclusion retain the same claims about training-free personalization of frozen VLAs, reference-based visual prompting, and benchmark effectiveness. The introduction's increased emphasis on temporal identity describes tracking already present in v2.

C2.justification: V3 adds interpretations contrasting persistent instance identity with spatial prompting, argues that tracking prevents cascading errors, and discusses parser flexibility and tolerance to occlusion and mask corruption. Appendix G adds mobile manipulation as a future direction. Existing cross-view and backbone limitations remain, although some new robustness interpretations overstate the accompanying numerical evidence.

D1.justification: New Tables 8–10 disclose track-specific episode counts, control frequencies, task horizons, and object properties, while consolidating previously described train/test separation. V3 also identifies the alternative parser and states a contrast-based tint-selection criterion. Hardware and backbone-training details remain unchanged. The front-page project-page link present in v2 is removed, reducing access information in the PDF.

R1.justification: V3 adds a focused Referring Object Manipulation discussion and six cited works, including VIMA, INVIGORATE, and Stone et al.'s open-world manipulation work. It sharpens the distinction between reference-based instance identity and other referring signals. MEMENTO remains the same cited work despite its title and publication update.

P1.justification: V3 selectively rewrites the introduction, problem explanation, and baseline rationale, adds Section 5.7 and appendix subsections, and revises appendix headings. Acknowledgements, an impact statement, and publication/correspondence information are added or updated. The overall organization and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: V3 substantially expands the tabular presentation with dedicated displays for parser performance, benchmark and split metadata, task specifications, occlusion, mask corruption, and dual-object results. The former Table 13 becomes the expanded, grouped Table 17. Existing Figures 1–24 are retained; table-caption placement, pagination, and figure locations also change, including Figure 24 moving after the discussion.

improvement.justification: The broader visual-prompt comparison, controlled robustness tests, and clearer benchmark documentation address useful gaps in v2's validation and reproducibility. The net gain is limited by incomplete descriptions of some new procedures and inaccurate numerical summaries. For example, Appendix E.5 claims tracking above 95% through three to four occluded frames, but Table 18 reports 94.0% for Bridge at three frames and below 90% for both platforms at four. The additions improve empirical scrutiny, while their interpretation requires greater care.
